brand_names: Palynziq (note: Palynziq is pegvaliase, a different drug — Kuvan is the correct brand for sapropterin)
what_its_for: Sapropterin is used to treat a condition called phenylketonuria (PKU). In PKU, your body cannot break down an amino acid called phenylalanine (Phe) properly, which can cause it to build up to harmful levels in your blood. This medicine helps your body break down phenylalanine more effectively, lowering the amount in your blood. It is used together with a low-phenylalanine diet — it does not replace the diet.
how_to_take: Take sapropterin by mouth, once a day, at the same time each day, with a meal to help your body absorb it better. The tablets can be dissolved in water or apple juice (4 to 8 ounces) if you have trouble swallowing them whole. Stir the drink until the tablets are fully dissolved or broken down, then drink it within 15 minutes. A few small pieces may remain in the drink — this is okay, go ahead and swallow them. You can also swallow the tablets whole if you prefer.
dosing: The dose is based on your body weight and is determined by your doctor. The usual starting dose is 10 mg per kilogram (kg) of body weight once a day. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well it works for you, measured by blood phenylalanine (Phe) levels. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on that same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next regular dose as scheduled. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store sapropterin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the tablets in their original bottle or foil pouch. Keep the lid tightly closed and protect the tablets from moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Do not use tablets that are past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Do not stop your low-phenylalanine diet unless your doctor tells you to — this medicine works best when used together with your prescribed diet. Avoid taking levodopa (a medicine for Parkinson's disease) at the same time without talking to your doctor first, as it may interact with sapropterin. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting sapropterin. Avoid becoming pregnant without first discussing it with your doctor, as PKU requires careful management during pregnancy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing; stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is severe or does not go away; headache, runny nose, or sore throat that worsens; unusual tiredness or weakness; or low blood phenylalanine levels (your doctor will monitor these). Also contact your doctor if your blood Phe levels do not improve after a few weeks on this medicine, as not everyone responds to sapropterin.
when_it_works: Sapropterin does not work for everyone with PKU — it only helps people whose PKU is caused by a type that responds to this medicine. Your doctor will check your blood phenylalanine levels after about 1 month of treatment to see if the medicine is working for you. If your Phe levels go down, the medicine is helping. If there is no response after 1 month at the proper dose, your doctor may decide to stop this medicine. If it does work, you will need to continue taking it regularly along with your diet to keep Phe levels under control.
special_populations: Children: Sapropterin can be used in children of all ages, including infants. Dosing is based on weight, so follow your child's doctor instructions carefully. Dissolving tablets in water or juice may make it easier for young children to take. Pregnancy: If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant and have PKU, it is very important to keep your blood Phe levels in a safe range, as high levels can harm your baby. Talk to your doctor immediately about managing your PKU during pregnancy. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as extra monitoring may be needed. Older Adults: There is limited information on use in elderly patients; your doctor will guide you based on your overall health.
